# ai-audit 
client  --->  ai-audit  --->  api.openai.com
                 |            api.anthropic.com
                 |  scan, redact or refuse
                 v
            audit.jsonl
         hash chain + anchor
[![CI](https://github.com/adagora/ai-audit/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/adagora/ai-audit/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://github.com/adagora/ai-audit/blob/main/LICENSE) [![Node](https://img.shields.io/badge/node-22.23%20%7C%2024.22%20%7C%2026.12%2B-339933)](https://github.com/adagora/ai-audit/blob/main/package.json)
Local proxy for the OpenAI and Anthropic HTTP APIs. It scans each request for secrets and personal data, masks or refuses the call, and appends a hash-chained audit record.
```bash git clone https://github.com/adagora/ai-audit.git && cd ai-audit && npm ci && npm run build && node dist/src/cli.js serve --mode redact --log audit.jsonl ```
There is no install script. This repository is not published on npm. `npm install -g ai-audit` installs a different program. ## TL;DR **The problem.** Agents and SDKs send prompts, tool results, screenshots and PDFs straight to the provider. A key or an IBAN in that payload is already gone. The record you can show later is whatever the provider kept. **The solution.** Point the client at `http://127.0.0.1:8787`. ai-audit scans the body, applies one of three modes, forwards only what that mode allows, and writes one `llm-call` line to a JSONL file. `ai-audit verify` recomputes the hash chain. `ai-audit anchor` writes a digest you store apart from the log, so a swapped or shortened file shows up. ### Why use ai-audit? | Behavior | What you get | |---|---| | `redact` | Text becomes `[REDACTED:rule]`. A hit in an image is blacked out. A hit in a PDF is rebuilt as page images. | | `no-go` | HTTP 409. The provider is never called. The response lists rule ids. | | `advisory` | The original body goes upstream. The finding is still in the log. | | Fail closed | A torn log, a full disk, or an attachment the proxy cannot read stops the call. | | Virtual keys | The client holds an `aia-` key. The provider key stays in the proxy process. | | Your log | JSONL on disk. One record per inspected call. A daily anchor file kept somewhere else. | | Overhead | About 0.6 to 0.7 ms p50 and about 1.1 ms p95 on a loopback mock, redaction included. See [the 2026-10-20 run](docs/performance/2026-10-20/README.md). | TypeScript, Node's standard library, no runtime dependencies. [Quinelings](https://github.com/CharlesHoskinson/quinelings) is optional and is not on the request path. Decisions are in [docs/adr](docs/adr/). ## Quick example For one local Codex session, run `npm run codex:proxy` from the repo root. It builds the proxy, asks for your OpenAI API key if `AI_AUDIT_UPSTREAM_OPENAI_KEY` is unset, generates a temporary `aia-` client key, starts the proxy on `127.0.0.1:8788`, and launches Codex through it. The provider key stays out of Codex's environment; the proxy stops when Codex exits. The audit log and proxy diagnostics stay in ignored `live/`. Set `AI_AUDIT_PORT=8787` if you have stopped the existing demo proxy and want the native Grafana scrape to follow this session. This launcher starts the proxy and Codex, not Grafana. ```bash git clone https://github.com/adagora/ai-audit.git cd ai-audit npm ci && npm run build keygen_out=$(node dist/src/cli.js keygen --name agent) client_key=$(printf '%s\n' "$keygen_out" | sed -n 's/^key (give to the client, not stored): //p') config_entry=$(printf '%s\n' "$keygen_out" | sed -n 's/^config entry: //p') printf '%s\n' "{\"keys\":[$config_entry]}" > gateway.json printf 'export AI_AUDIT_CLIENT_KEY=%s\n' "$client_key" export AI_AUDIT_UPSTREAM_OPENAI_KEY="sk-your-provider-key"

# AI Act – AI decision log (prototype)

> **Not legal advice. Unverified.** The mapping below is an engineering reading of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689
> (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), written from memory. Check article wording and dates (including changes proposed in the "Digital Omnibus") against EUR-Lex and with a lawyer.

## What applies to whom

| Article | Summary | Scope | Feature here |
|---|---|---|---|
| Art. 12 | High-risk systems must technically allow automatic recording of events (logs) over their lifetime, for traceability and post-market monitoring. | **high-risk only** | `record()`: timestamp, system, use case, input hash, sources (doc/page), model + version, prompt template hash, parameters, output |
| Art. 19 (provider), Art. 26(6) (deployer) | Automatically generated logs are kept for at least **6 months**, unless other law (e.g. GDPR) says otherwise. | **high-risk only** | append-only JSONL + hash chain (`verifyChain()`); `rotate` into linked segments and `prune --keep-days N` with a recorded prune ([ADR 0049](docs/adr/0049-log-segments-and-retention.md)); choosing N is the operator's job |
| Art. 13 | Transparency to the deployer: instructions, capabilities, limits, how to interpret output, logging mechanisms. | **high-risk only** | `report()`: models, sources, stats — input for documentation |
| Art. 14 | Human oversight: ability to understand, disregard, override or reverse the output. | **high-risk only** | `approve()`: reviewer, decision (approved/overridden/rejected), time; override rate in report |
| Art. 50 | Users must know they talk to an AI; generated content marked machine-readably; deepfakes/public texts disclosed. | **broad** — any chatbot / generator (from 2 Aug 2026) | outside the log; in middleware: "AI answer" banner + metadata flag |
| Art. 4 | AI literacy of staff. | **broad**, from 2 Feb 2025 | mention only — training, not code |

Most company RAG systems (docs, translation, quoting) are **not** high-risk (Annex III: e.g. HR/recruitment, credit, critical infrastructure; Annex I: safety components of products). Then mainly Art. 50 and 4 are mandatory, and the log is good practice (traceability, ISO/IEC 42001, readiness if the system becomes high-risk).

## GDPR
By default only `sha256(input)` is stored. Optionally `redactedInput` (masks e-mail, phone, PESEL — simple heuristic, no guarantee). Hashes of short data can be reversed with a dictionary — use a keyed HMAC in production.

## Quinelings (Apache-2.0)
**Gives:** the idea that a decision step is a bounded (step-limited), deterministic program with exact source, so it can be reproduced and re-run. Here: `step.sourceHash` + `replay()` in `node:vm` with step and time limits, plus the optional QDL path.
**Does not give:** logs, retention, integrity chain, human oversight, reports, transparency (Art. 50), or compliance out of the box.

## Prototype limits
- Local file: the hash chain detects edits/deletions; swapping the whole file needs anchors (`ai-audit anchor`, keep them elsewhere, e.g. WORM/S3 Object Lock).
- The `steps` registry for vm replay is in memory; QDL records are self-contained.
- `node:vm` is not a security sandbox — only for your own trusted step code.
- The deterministic step is reproducible, the LLM answer is not (it is only logged).

# Deterministic decisions (optional, Quinelings, Node ≥ 22)
**TL;DR: where Quinelings helps this project**
- **Reproduces how a decision was calculated, long after.** The log carries the decision program itself. `ai-audit replay` rebuilds it from the log alone and recomputes the result, and `ai-audit policies` shows which policy version decided and what changed since. This does not authenticate the input facts or establish that the rule was wise.
- **Compares two rules on one recorded session.** `npm run example:lab` replays two session governors over the same proxy log, shows the first decision where they disagree, and reruns a changed threshold in a fresh process ([ADR 0035](adr/0035-read-only-session-policy-comparison.md)).
- **Runs a fixed program, safely.** A program always stops, cannot read files or the network, and is refused if it invents an operation or mixes up units. The built-in `replay()` runs JavaScript in `node:vm`, which is only safe for trusted code.
- **Keeps secrets out of the evidence.** Inputs and programs are checked with the proxy's rules before anything runs; a customer e-mail or an API key stops the decision instead of landing in the log.
- **Keeps the hard cases and shows real use.** Refused and failed evaluations are recorded too, each decision links to the proxied LLM call (`llmCallId` is the proxy's `x-request-id`), and when agents run Quinelings on their own through MCP, the proxy logs which programs they compiled and ran, as hashes only.
- **Not for** the proxy's request path (one run takes ~20 ms against the proxy's ~0.6 ms), finding secrets or PII, making the LLM itself reproducible, or real actions (they are only simulated).

[Quinelings](https://github.com/CharlesHoskinson/quinelings) (`@quinelings/agent-sdk`, Apache-2.0, vendored in `vendor/`) runs small calculation programs written in QDL, a JSON format: typed inputs with units, steps from a fixed set of about 30 operations (`arithmetic`, `compareValues`, `budget`, `allocate`, `action`, …) and outputs. The SDK compiles a program into self-contained source whose hash is its identity (`ql_…`), checks types and units before anything runs, and can rebuild and rerun it anywhere from that source alone. A program is data, not JavaScript, and `action` steps are only simulated.

## The SDK on its own
Save as `qdl-hello.mjs` in the repo root and run `node qdl-hello.mjs`:
```js
import { Session } from "@quinelings/agent-sdk/v1";

const session = new Session();
const program = session.compile({
  format: "qdl-intent", version: 1, name: "Quote with a floor",
  thought: "price = max(machining minutes × shop rate, 150 PLN)",
  inputs: [
    { id: "minutes", name: "minutes", type: { kind: "number", unit: "min", min: 0 } },
    { id: "rate", name: "rate", type: { kind: "number", unit: "PLN*min^-1", min: 0 } },
    { id: "floor", value: 150, type: { kind: "number", unit: "PLN", min: 0 } },
  ],
  steps: [
    { id: "machining", op: "arithmetic", inputs: ["minutes", "rate"], params: { kind: "mul" } },
    { id: "price", op: "arithmetic", inputs: ["machining", "floor"], params: { kind: "max" } },
  ],
  outputs: ["price"],
});
const run = session.run({ artifactId: program.id, requestId: "quote-1", inputs: { minutes: 42, rate: 4.5 } });
console.log(run.result.occurrences[0].outputs);
console.log(new Session().recover({ source: program.source }).id === program.id);
```
It prints `[ 189 ]`, then `true`: a fresh session rebuilt the same program from its source. Bad programs and inputs are refused with a `QdlError` before anything runs: mixed-up units (`unit-type`), a value outside its declared range such as `minutes: -5` (`refinement`), a missing input (`missing-input`) or an operation that does not exist, for example an LLM inventing a `fetch` step (`invalid-input`). Errors at run time, such as division by zero, give a `failed` run with a diagnostic.

# 2. Hash-chained JSONL audit log with external anchors
Status: Accepted (2026-10-20)
## Context
The log must show that records were not edited or deleted (AI Act Art. 12/19 traceability), without a database.
## Decision
Append-only JSONL where each record carries the hash of the previous one. `lastHash` is read from the end of the file, not by loading the whole log: O(1) per write, and safe when CLI `approve` writes while the proxy runs.
`ai-audit anchor` appends `{ts,count,head}` to a separate append-only file. `verify --anchors` uses it to catch a recomputed (swapped) chain and truncation.
## Consequences
- The chain alone detects edits and deletions, not replacement of the whole file.
- Anchors only help if the anchors file lives elsewhere (e.g. WORM / S3 Object Lock). That is the operator's job.
- Stats and reports are computed from this log, the single source of truth.

# 46. A deterministic gate checks proposed tool calls before the client receives them
Status: Accepted (2026-10-29). Extends [0009](0009-inspect-whole-request.md); keeps [0045](0045-local-advisory-injection-judge.md) advisory.
## Context
Blocking on injection-like content is too slow or too inaccurate for the request path. On 36 synthetic cases the regex rules missed 7 of 18 attacks. The local Qwen judge took 2–11 s per tool result on an M1 and flagged 1 of 24 ordinary repository chunks. False blocks compound per session: at 4% per tool result, 50 results stop about 87% of sessions; at 1%, about 40%. Adaptive attackers defeat content classifiers. Harm starts when the agent acts. The proxy already parses the client-executed tool calls in each response (`src/extract.ts`), but delivers the response unchanged.
## Decision
- An optional `actionGate` in `gateway.json` lists tools by exact name. Each entry has `mode` (`observe` or `enforce`), sensitive `arguments` as JSON paths (`$`, `$.to`) and an `allow` list: a host, `*.domain` for its subdomains, an email address, `@domain`, a phone number or an IBAN. Unlisted tools pass unchecked. Without `actionGate` nothing changes.
- For each call to a listed tool, fixed rules take atoms from the string values under its arguments: hosts of URLs with a scheme, a whole value shaped like a hostname, and the scanner's email, phone and IBAN matches as destinations; every other scanner match is a finding. No model runs.
- Origin of an atom: `user` if it occurs in user message text; `system` if only in system, developer or instructions text; `untrusted` if only in tool results, tool definitions or assistant turns; `none` if nowhere; `unknown` when the provider holds the history (`previous_response_id`, `conversation`). Client system prompts name many hosts, so `system` does not pass.
- A destination passes if it is allowed or its origin is `user`. A finding never passes. Arguments that are not a JSON object fail. A call fails if one atom fails.
- `observe` delivers the response unchanged and records what would be held. `enforce` holds every tool call of a response that contains a failed call and ends the response as a text answer with a normal stop reason, naming the tool and `audit_action_held`. Text parts stream without delay; tool-call parts wait for the end of the response. Non-streaming responses are rewritten the same way.
- The `llm-call` record gets `actionGate.calls`: tool, call index, mode, result and, per atom, argument path, kind, origin, the source path of an untrusted occurrence, whether it was allowed and its result. Never a value or its hash ([0007](0007-log-stores-no-values.md)). The gate configuration enters `configDigest` ([0014](0014-versioned-inspection-profiles.md)). `/metrics` counts calls by mode and result.
- Injection signals and model judgments never decide the gate; they remain advisory evidence beside its results. Quinelings is not on this path; richer policies are compared offline in `lab`.
## Consequences
- The gate stops sends, uploads and payments to destinations that untrusted content supplied, and secrets placed in actions, in any language or wording, at microsecond cost and without a model.
- It does not see provider-executed tools, unlisted tools, answers changed without a tool call, or destinations the user also typed. Shell commands are covered only through URLs with a scheme, addresses and findings in them. An attacker can still use an allowed destination.
- A legitimate destination read from a tool result (an address from a CRM lookup) is held until it is allowed or the user types it. Observe mode measures this friction before enforcement.
- The proxy rewrites responses for the first time. Three streaming formats gain parsing, replacement code and tests. Clients receive tool-call arguments at once instead of streamed.
- `enforce` fails closed for listed tools; unparsable arguments hold the call.

# 49. The audit log rotates into linked segments; old segments leave only by a recorded prune
Status: Accepted (2026-10-29). Extends [0002](0002-hash-chained-log-with-anchors.md), [0016](0016-fail-closed-when-log-unavailable.md), [0018](0018-keyed-session-linking.md) and [0026](0026-store-each-program-once.md).
## Context
The log is one file that only grows. The proxy rebuilt its session index at start with one `readFileSync` of the whole file, and the CLI readers (`verify`, `report`, `stats`, `context`, `workbench`, `decide`, `replay`, `receipt`, `policies`) read it the same way. Node cannot hold a string above 536,870,888 characters; at about 1.7 KB per `llm-call` that is roughly 300,000 records, weeks of traffic for a team of agents. Past it, session linking stopped with only a counter, and the CLI readers crashed. AI Act Art. 19 and 26(6) ask deployers of high-risk systems to keep logs for at least six months, and data protection asks to delete them afterwards. There was no way to do either without editing the chained file, which `verify` reports as tampering.
## Decision
- Rotation closes the current file and starts a new one. While holding `<log>.lock`, it renames `audit.jsonl` to `audit.<UTC time of rotation>.jsonl` (stem, compact ISO time with milliseconds, extension) and writes the first record of a new `audit.jsonl`: `{kind: "segment", previous: {file, count, head}}`, where `head` is the last hash of the closed file. Each file chains from genesis on its own. `<log>.lock`, `<log>.session-key` and `<log>.budgets` keep their names. A torn last line is not rotated.
- `ai-audit rotate --log LOG` rotates on demand, for example daily next to `anchor`. `serve` rotates before an append when the file is larger than `--rotate-bytes`, default 256 MiB, 0 to disable. An append to a missing file next to closed segments first writes the `segment` record, so a file moved aside by hand, or a rotation cut short after its rename, continues the series. Rotation runs under the append lock; a failure is a log failure under ADR 0016.
- A log path names a series: closed segments with the same stem in the same directory, ordered by name, then the current file. `verify` and every reader take the series. `verify` checks each file's chain and each `segment` record against the file before it, and names the file of a break. An anchor matches the file that holds a record with its count and head.
- Readers stream each file line by line, so no file has to fit in one string. They read the whole series: reading only the segments of an interval is left for later, because a call is appended when it ends and can land after a rotation that followed its start. The proxy rebuilds its session index from the newest closed segment and the current file.
- An `AuditLog` that remembers which programs it stored (ADR 0026) forgets them when the current file changes, so each segment gets its own `program` record. `replay` looks for a program anywhere in the series.
- `ai-audit prune --log LOG --keep-days N` deletes the oldest closed segments whose last record is older than N days. It refuses a series that does not verify. It first appends a content-free `prune` record to the current file with each segment's name, record count, head, and first and last time, then deletes them. A missing first segment that no `prune` record lists is a break, and so is any missing segment after it. Anchors older than the first kept segment that match no kept file are counted as pruned, not failed. There is no default retention and no automatic deletion: the operator sets N; any six months fit in 184 days.
## Consequences
- No file grows much past the rotation size, and no reader needs a file to fit in one string. A six-month series at the default size is a few hundred files.
- CLI readers still hold every record of the series in memory. A long series needs a machine with that memory, or a later change that reads only the segments of an interval.

# Workflow cockpit

The local console has two modes. The synthetic page runs fixed checks through the proxy with fake keys and a mock provider. The real page calls OpenAI through a separate `ai-audit serve` process. The provider key never goes to browser JavaScript. Both pages show each request's client context, the after-policy view, role byte composition, decision, usage, history and telemetry. The real page's after-policy view is scanner-derived; its audit log does not store prompt values.

## Real OpenAI workflow

```sh
npm run example:workflow:real
```

The launcher reads `AI_AUDIT_UPSTREAM_OPENAI_KEY` or `OPENAI_API_KEY` from the environment, then `OPENAI_API_KEY` from the repository's untracked `.env`. If none is set, it prompts for the key in the terminal without echoing it. Open `http://127.0.0.1:8791`, choose an OpenAI model available to your API key, and send two prompts. The second request carries the previous turn so the proxy can link the session. Use **New conversation** to start another one. The page uses a generated virtual client key, so OpenAI sees the provider key only from the proxy. Actual API use can incur charges.

The terminal prints the proxy base URL, a generated `aia-` virtual key, and the real audit log path. Keep the terminal open. The proxy runs on `http://127.0.0.1:8792/v1` by default; set `WORKFLOW_REAL_PROXY_PORT` and `WORKFLOW_REAL_PAGE_PORT` before launch to use other ports. The page does not serve real log data. Inspect it offline:

```sh
node dist/src/cli.js verify --log live/workflow-real.jsonl
node dist/src/cli.js context --log live/workflow-real.jsonl
node dist/src/cli.js workbench --log live/workflow-real.jsonl --output /private/tmp/ai-audit-real-workbench.html
```

Choose a new workbench output filename for each export. The generated HTML is private and should be opened locally. It summarizes recorded metadata, including scan history, sessions, context composition and Quinelings observation.

## Use UniiChat as a real client

While the real workflow launcher is running, open a second terminal and use the `aia-` key printed by the launcher:

```sh
cd path/to/uniichat
export OPENAI_API_KEY='aia-key-printed-by-the-workflow-launcher'
export UNII_OPENAI_BASE='http://127.0.0.1:8792/v1'
export UNII_VENDORS='openai-api'
export UNII_PICK='openai-api:YOUR_MODEL:medium:slow'
export UNII_COMPACTOR='openai-api:YOUR_MODEL:medium:slow'
bun Server.ts
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:8788`. These variables configure UniiChat's OpenAI calls through ai-audit; the `OPENAI_API_KEY` value in this terminal is the generated **virtual** key, not your provider key. UniiChat's `/v1/responses` requests pass through the proxy. Other UniiChat routes, such as `/v1/audio/transcriptions`, are outside the proxy's current route set. UniiChat keeps its own conversation history, while ai-audit keeps metadata in its audit log.

## Synthetic coverage

```sh
npm run example:workflow
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:8790` for the dashboard. It refreshes every two seconds and shows request rates by outcome, latency, scan findings, injection signals, tool-call gate results, refusals, usage and the audit chain of all three synthetic proxies. Its test bench runs each feature check against the real proxy handler and marks it pass or fail against the expected result; **Run all checks** runs every one. Select a check or a log row to see the stored, content-free record. The request console described below is at `http://127.0.0.1:8790/console`.

# Monitoring example

VictoriaMetrics scrapes the proxy's `/metrics`. Grafana shows a live operations and evidence dashboard, evaluates alert rules, and ntfy delivers the alerts. Everything is provisioned from files in this folder, and all images are pinned. The dashboard source is `grafana/build-dashboard.mjs`; run `node grafana/build-dashboard.mjs` to regenerate its provisioned JSON.

| Service | Image | URL |
|---|---|---|
| proxy | built from `../../Dockerfile` | http://127.0.0.1:8787 |
| mock-upstream | `node:26.12.1-slim` | internal only |
| victoriametrics | `victoriametrics/victoria-metrics:v1.154.1` | http://127.0.0.1:8428 |
| grafana | `grafana/grafana:13.2.4` | http://127.0.0.1:3000 |
| ntfy | `binwiederhier/ntfy:v2.32.0` | http://127.0.0.1:8080 |

The proxy forwards to `mock-upstream`, so no provider keys are needed and nothing leaves the host.

For real Codex traffic, use the `docker-compose.real.yml` override. It changes the proxy upstream to OpenAI, injects the provider key only into the proxy, and keeps Grafana scraping that same proxy. The mock service may start because it is a dependency of the base demo Compose file, but it receives no Codex requests.

For a native run outside Docker, start the mock with `MOCK_UPSTREAM_HOST=127.0.0.1` so it listens on loopback only.

For a single real Codex session without Docker, run `npm run codex:proxy` from the repository root. It starts a temporary real-provider proxy on port 8788 and launches Codex. Set `AI_AUDIT_PORT=8787` after stopping the demo proxy if you want the native VictoriaMetrics scrape to follow that Codex session. The launcher does not start Grafana or VictoriaMetrics.

## Run

```sh
cd examples/monitoring
NTFY_TOPIC=ai-audit-alerts GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD=change-me docker compose up -d --build
```

Real-provider mode, after creating an `aia-` key with `node dist/src/cli.js keygen --name codex`:

```sh
export AI_AUDIT_UPSTREAM_OPENAI_KEY='your-OpenAI-API-key'
export AI_AUDIT_CLIENT_KEY='your-aia-virtual-key'
export NTFY_TOPIC='choose-a-private-topic'
export GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD='choose-a-password'
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.real.yml up -d --build
```

Run this from `examples/monitoring`. Start Codex from a second shell with the custom provider command in the [README](../../README.md#quick-example), using the same `aia-` key. `docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.real.yml logs -f proxy` follows the proxy. The dashboard remains at `http://127.0.0.1:3000`.

- Grafana: log in as `admin` with `GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD`. The dashboard is in the `ai-audit` folder.
- ntfy: open http://127.0.0.1:8080/ai-audit-alerts, or subscribe to the topic in the ntfy app.
- `NTFY_TOPIC` selects the topic. Anyone who knows a topic name can read it, so use a hard-to-guess name if ntfy is reachable from other machines.

## Dashboard and evidence

The dashboard covers request decisions and latency, audit-log failures, prompt-injection signals, attachment and sandbox state, session-index health, upstream failures, missing token usage, and observed Quinelings tool activity. The selected Grafana time range controls the overview counts. A scrape-health panel separates a healthy proxy from missing telemetry.

`/metrics` has bounded aggregate labels. It does not contain session IDs, individual context maps, log entries, token totals, QDL verdicts, or source values. Those belong in the local hash-chained log. Use the dashboard to find a time window and failure mode, then use the CLI for the individual evidence:

```sh
docker compose exec proxy node dist/src/cli.js verify --log /data/audit.jsonl
docker compose exec proxy node dist/src/cli.js context --log /data/audit.jsonl
docker compose exec proxy node dist/src/cli.js context --log /data/audit.jsonl --session SESSION_ID --output /data/session.html
docker compose cp proxy:/data/session.html ./session.html
